In August 2014, the WHO Director-General declared the Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) outbreak in West Africa a Public Health Emergency of International Concern under the International Health Regulations (IHR) 2005. Temporary recommendations for countries with Ebola transmission included conducting exit screening at international airports, seaports, and major land crossings to identify individuals with unexplained febrile illness consistent with potential EVD infection. Exit screening should minimally include a questionnaire, temperature measurement, and risk assessment for fever caused by EVD. Individuals with symptoms consistent with EVD should not travel unless as part of a medical evacuation. International travel of EVD contacts or cases is prohibited unless medically evacuated. Exit screening is a public health intervention designed to identify individuals with possible symptoms of or exposure to EVD and prevent their further travel. Screening measures are based on symptom assessment and risk evaluation and can be adapted for airports, ports, and land crossings. Effective exit screening helps prevent the spread of disease to other areas, protects travelers and crew, and complies with public health recommendations. Travelers are assessed for signs and symptoms of EVD or identified as contacts potentially exposed to the virus. Laboratory testing to confirm EVD is not feasible during exit screening. Before implementing exit screening, a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) should be developed in consultation with stakeholders, including government entities, public health authorities, civil aviation and maritime authorities, airport or port managers, conveyance operators, and security personnel. These entities will lead the implementation of the screening process and manage resources. Separate SOPs may be required for different facilities. Departure terminals warranting exit screening, primary and secondary screening locations, staffing and training needs, and necessary supplies (e.g., non-contact thermometers, personal protective equipment [PPE], communication materials) should be identified. Travelers should undergo exit screening as early as possible upon arrival at the facility, in conjunction with existing security procedures. Exit screening should include a public health communication campaign to educate travelers and the travel industry. Messages should inform travelers about the outbreak, the intent to screen for EVD symptoms and exposure risk, and the following key points: Sick travelers should postpone travel. Those with symptoms consistent with EVD will not be allowed to travel unless medically evacuated. Travelers should arrive early at the facility and expect delays due to public health screening. Completion of a Traveler Public Health Declaration is required, and questionnaires will be reviewed before boarding clearance. Temperature measurement will be conducted in addition to normal security procedures. Boarding may be denied based on public health criteria. Primary screening identifies travelers who may be symptomatic with or exposed to EVD. Personnel without public health or medical training can conduct this initial screening, which includes observing travelers for signs of illness, measuring temperature, and reviewing public health questionnaires to determine risk. Travelers exhibiting signs or symptoms of EVD, reporting fever, or answering yes to any questionnaire item should be referred to secondary screening for further evaluation. Boarding is refused until secondary screening is completed. Secondary screening involves further evaluation of travelers identified during primary screening as potentially ill or exposed to EVD. This process should be conducted by personnel with public health or medical training. Travelers referred to secondary screening should not be allowed to board until a comprehensive risk assessment is completed.
